title: The app this page links to isn't in the store
what: An App Store or Google Play link on the page names an app the store no longer has.
why: Visitors who tap "Get the app" land on an error page. Apps disappear when they are renamed, moved to a new developer account or pulled.
fix: Link to the app's current store page, or remove the link if the app is gone.
tech: the iTunes Lookup API returns no result for the id (in the link's storefront and in the US), or the Google Play listing answers 404. A 429 or a regional-only app is could-not-check, not dead

title: Links on this page go nowhere
what: Links to other pages on the site return an error (404, 410 or 5xx).
why: Visitors who click hit a dead end, and search engines take broken links as a sign the site is neglected.
fix: Point each link at the page's current address, or remove it. When a page moved, add a 301 redirect from the old address.
tech: a sampled same-site a[href] ends in 4xx (not 401, 403 or 429) or 5xx. A 200 page that says "not found" (a soft 404) is out of scope

title: This page tells Google to show a different page
what: The page's canonical tag names a different address as the real one.
why: Search engines treat the page as a copy, so it may never appear in results.
fix: Give each page a canonical tag that points at its own address. Shared SEO components are the usual cause.
tech: <link rel="canonical"> on the page points at another URL

title: This page has two titles
what: The HTML has more than one title element (titles inside SVG images do not count).
why: Search engines pick one, not always the one you meant, so the result shows the wrong title. It usually means two SEO components both render one.
fix: Keep one <title> in the head. Remove the one a theme, plugin or layout adds on top of your SEO component.
tech: more than one <title> element outside <svg>

title: The page and the calendar disagree about an event
what: An event in the page's structured data has a different start time, name or place than the .ics calendar entry on the same day.
why: Search results, the page and guests' phone calendars each show one of the two versions, so some guests turn up at the wrong time.
fix: Correct whichever is wrong, then generate both from one source so they cannot drift.
tech: Event JSON-LD and an .ics occurrence on the same local date: matched by normalised name, then start time and location compared; a lone occurrence that day with another name is reported as renamed

title: The page still promotes an event that already happened
what: An event in the page's structured data, or a card marked as the next or upcoming event, is dated before now.
why: Guests plan around the date on the page. A night that already happened, still shown as next, sends people to a closed room or to a different night.
fix: Update the card and the structured data when an event ends. Generating both from the calendar keeps them current.
tech: an Event's endDate (or startDate when there is none) is before the run time, or a next/upcoming element's time[datetime] is; dates are read in the venue's time zone

title: The feed this page advertises is broken
what: The page links to an RSS or Atom feed that returns an error (4xx or 5xx).
why: Feed readers, podcast apps and newsletter tools that follow the site stop getting new posts, usually without anyone noticing.
fix: Restore the feed at that address, or update the link rel="alternate" tag to where the feed lives now.
tech: an advertised feed returns 4xx or 5xx

title: Your whole site exists at two addresses
what: Both www and the bare domain load the site, instead of one redirecting to the other.
why: Search engines can split your ranking between two copies of every page.
fix: Pick one address and 301-redirect the other to it at your host or DNS provider.
tech: the alternate host returns 200 instead of 301

title: This page's HTML is enormous
what: The HTML of the page alone is over 2 MB, before any image, script or stylesheet.
why: Phones on slow connections wait seconds before anything shows, and search engines may stop reading the page before the end.
fix: Find what fills the HTML: usually a framework data payload, inlined SVG or CSS, or a long list rendered in full. Load it on demand or paginate it.
tech: the UTF-8 HTML body is over 2 MB (2,097,152 bytes); html-heavy is not reported for the same page

title: Your calendar shows the wrong hour on some phones
what: Events in your .ics calendar have a start time with no time zone (no TZID and no Z).
why: Phones read such a time in the guest's own zone, so anyone in another zone, or travelling, sees the event at the wrong hour.
fix: Give each DTSTART a time zone, for example DTSTART;TZID=America/Los_Angeles:20261112T190000. Most calendar exports have a time zone setting.
tech: a VEVENT's DTSTART has neither TZID nor a trailing Z (a floating time, RFC 5545 §3.3.5); all-day VALUE=DATE events are not reported

title: Some images on this page don't load
what: An image on the site (or the original behind a Next.js /_next/image address) returns an error.
why: Visitors see an empty box or a broken-image icon where a product photo or a diagram should be.
fix: Upload the image again, or point the img at its current address. For /_next/image, check the file named by url= exists.
tech: a sampled same-site img src answers 4xx or 5xx (images on other hosts are not requested)

title: Structured data points at pages that don't exist
what: Addresses on the site named in the page's structured data (a product URL, an image, a logo) return an error.
why: Search engines use these addresses for rich results. A dead product or image address can drop the rich result entirely.
fix: Update the structured data to the current addresses. Generated structured data usually means a stale CMS field or a renamed route.
tech: same-site http(s) strings inside JSON-LD answer 4xx or 5xx; at most 12 are requested, the first 12 in document order

title: This page's structured data is broken
what: A structured data block (script type="application/ld+json") is not valid JSON.
why: Search engines ignore the whole block, so prices, reviews, FAQs or opening hours in it never reach the results.
fix: Fix the JSON in that block: usually a trailing comma, an unescaped quote or a template that printed nothing. Paste it into a JSON validator to find the line.
tech: JSON.parse fails on a script type="application/ld+json" block (one finding per block)

title: Prices differ between language versions
what: The same item (matched by its structured data sku, or name) shows a different price on another language version of the page.
why: Customers see one price and pay another, or compare the two versions and stop trusting either.
fix: Update the price on every version, ideally from one product record. A version that was copied and translated keeps last month's price.
tech: Product or Offer price in JSON-LD (then the configured priceSelector; never free text) differs for one sku across versions; "$12", "12 USD" and "$12.00" are equal

title: Test content is on the live site
what: The page's main content shows test or sample content: a test product, a sample post, John Doe, an example.com email address or a 555 phone number.
why: Unlike placeholder copy, a visitor can act on it: buy the test product, email the example address or call the fake number.
fix: Delete or unpublish the test entries in the CMS or shop, and replace sample contact details with real ones.
tech: main content (code and pre ignored) contains "test product", "sample product", "sample post", "sample page", "test post", "hello world!", "john doe", "jane doe", "john smith example", "your name here", "product name here", an @example.com/.org/.net address, or a 555 phone number (English lists)

title: This page asks search engines not to list it
what: The page has a robots meta tag containing noindex.
why: If that isn't on purpose, the page is invisible in search.
fix: Remove noindex from pages you want found.
tech: <meta name="robots" content="noindex">

title: Assistants find two different names for your business
what: The business name in the page's structured data and the title of /llms.txt are not the same name.
why: Assistants match a question to a business by name. Two names can make them treat one business as two, or quote the wrong one.
fix: Use the same business name in the LocalBusiness structured data and as the first heading of llms.txt.
tech: LocalBusiness JSON-LD name and the llms.txt H1 disagree (case, punctuation and a leading "The" ignored)

title: Your robots.txt tells every search engine to stay away
what: robots.txt has a group for every crawler (User-agent: *) that disallows the whole site.
why: Search engines stop crawling the site, so new pages never appear and old ones fade out of results.
fix: Remove the Disallow: / line from the User-agent: * group, or replace it with the paths you mean to hide. This line is often left over from a staging site.
tech: robots.txt: User-agent: * with Disallow: / and no Allow that overrides it

title: Your organization has more than one identity in structured data
what: The Organization or WebSite @id differs from the one in your schema guide, or differs from page to page.
why: Search engines join structured data across pages by @id. Two ids make two organizations, splitting what is known about yours.
fix: Use one fixed @id for the Organization and one for the WebSite on every page, for example https://example.com/#organization.
tech: an Organization or WebSite @id (compared after resolving and trimming a trailing slash) differs from organizationId/websiteId, or, with no guide, differs between the sampled pages

title: Your sitemap lists pages that don't exist
what: Pages listed in the sitemap return an error (4xx or 5xx).
why: The sitemap is where you tell search engines which pages matter. Dead entries waste their visits and make them trust the sitemap less.
fix: Remove the dead addresses from the sitemap, or restore the pages. A generated sitemap usually means a deleted page is still in the CMS or the route list.
tech: sampled sitemap entries return 4xx or 5xx

title: Hidden editing characters leaked onto the live site
what: The title, a meta tag or the structured data contains invisible characters: Unicode tag characters or long runs of zero-width characters, the kind a CMS preview (such as Sanity's stega) adds.
why: They are invisible to you but not to everyone else: search results, share previews and copied text carry them, and they can break string comparisons and structured data.
fix: Turn stega encoding off for production builds (in Sanity, set stega: false outside preview) and strip it from fields that end up in metadata.
tech: a code point in U+E0000 to U+E007F, or 4 or more zero-width characters in a row, in the title, meta content or JSON-LD strings

title: Google sees an almost empty page
what: Fewer than 60 words exist in the page before JavaScript runs, outside the header, nav and footer.
why: Many crawlers and AI tools read the page without running JavaScript, so they see almost nothing.
fix: Render the main content on the server. In Next.js, keep it out of client-only components and Suspense boundaries that wait for the browser.
tech: word count of server-rendered HTML

title: The iPhone app banner promotes a different app
what: The page's Smart App Banner (the apple-itunes-app meta tag) names a different app id than the page's App Store link.
why: Safari shows the banner at the top of the page on iPhone, so visitors install whichever app it names, which here is not the one the page links to.
fix: Set app-id in the apple-itunes-app meta tag to the same id as the App Store link.
tech: <meta name="apple-itunes-app" content="app-id=..."> differs from every apps.apple.com/.../id<digits> link on the page

title: An event at your venue lists a different address
what: An event the page says is at the venue (by the venue's name or id) gives a different street address than the venue's own structured data.
why: Maps and search results send guests to the event's address, so a stale one sends them to the wrong door.
fix: Use the venue's own address in each event's location, ideally by referring to the venue's @id instead of repeating it.
tech: Event location names the LocalBusiness (same name or @id) and its address differs by house number or ZIP

title: The feed this page advertises is not a feed
what: The advertised feed address answers, but with something that is not RSS or Atom, often an HTML page.
why: Feed readers cannot read it, so subscribers get nothing. A framework's catch-all route is the usual cause.
fix: Serve the feed's XML at that address, or point the link rel="alternate" tag at the address that does.
tech: the feed body does not start with an XML declaration, <rss> or <feed>

title: The feed this page advertises is too large
what: The feed response is larger than 2 MB.
why: Feed readers and aggregators time out or truncate large feeds, and frameworks such as Next.js do not cache responses over 2 MB, so every request rebuilds it.
fix: Limit the feed to recent items (20 to 50 is typical) and put a summary in each item instead of the full post.
tech: the feed response is larger than 2 MB (2,097,152 bytes)

title: A language version doesn't link back
what: This page's hreflang points at a version in another language, but that version's hreflang doesn't point back.
why: Search engines ignore hreflang pairs that aren't confirmed from both sides, so searchers may get the wrong language.
fix: Give every version the same full set of hreflang links, including one to itself.
tech: page A has <link rel=alternate hreflang> to B, and B (fetched) has none to A (a trailing slash is not a difference)

title: Most of this page's HTML is a data payload
what: More than half of the HTML, and over 300 KB, is inline data (JSON, __NEXT_DATA__ or a framework's streamed payload) rather than content.
why: Every visitor downloads data the page may never show, and it delays the first paint on phones.
fix: Send only the fields the page renders. In Next.js, trim what getServerSideProps or a server component passes to client components.
tech: inline data scripts are over 300 KB (307,200 bytes) and more than half the HTML; not reported when html-huge is

title: Your calendar names a time zone it doesn't describe
what: Events in your .ics calendar use a TZID, but the file has no VTIMEZONE section for it.
why: The iCalendar standard requires the description. Some calendar apps fall back to UTC or the guest's zone without it, and show the wrong hour.
fix: Export the calendar with time zone definitions included, or add a VTIMEZONE for each TZID the events use.
tech: a DTSTART or DTEND TZID has no matching VTIMEZONE component (RFC 5545 §3.6.5)

title: Images are requested at an enormous width
what: An image is offered or requested 3840 pixels wide or more, wider than almost any screen shows it.
why: Phones and laptops may download a 4K-wide picture to show it a few hundred pixels across, which wastes data and slows the page.
fix: Cap the widths your image component generates (for Next.js, deviceSizes and imageSizes in next.config) and set the sizes attribute.
tech: a srcset candidate with a w descriptor, or a w= parameter, of 3840 or more

title: None of the images on this page are described
what: The page has images, and not one has alt text that says what it shows.
why: Screen reader users hear nothing about any picture, and search engines have no words to index the images by.
fix: Give each meaningful image an alt that says what it shows. alt="" is right for decorative images, but a page where every image is decorative is rare.
tech: every img has a missing, empty or whitespace-only alt

title: Some images are very large files
what: An image on the page is over 500 KB.
why: Large images are the most common reason a page is slow on a phone, and a slow page loses visitors before it loads.
fix: Resize the image to the size it is shown at and export it as WebP or AVIF, or serve it through an image CDN or your framework's image component.
tech: a sampled image's Content-Length header is over 512,000 bytes; a server that sends no Content-Length gives no finding

title: Images still load from an old WordPress site
what: Images on the page are served from /wp-content/uploads/, usually left over from a WordPress site the new site replaced.
why: When the old WordPress install or its host is switched off, every one of these images breaks at once.
fix: Move the images into the new site's own media library or asset folder and update the addresses.
tech: img src or srcset candidates under /wp-content/uploads/

title: A language version of this page is missing
what: The page says (through hreflang, the sitemap or your language settings) that it has a version in another language, but that version returns an error or redirects to the homepage.
why: Visitors who switch language land on an error or on the homepage, and search engines drop the alternate from results.
fix: Publish the missing version, or remove it from the page's hreflang links and the sitemap. Pages meant to exist in one language only can be excluded in gaugeline.languages.json.
tech: an expected twin (hreflang, sitemap xhtml:link or the configured prefix, subdomain or parameter) answers 4xx or 5xx, or redirects to / or a language root; at most 5 versions are fetched

title: Some links go through a link shortener
what: Links leave the page through a shortener or redirector (bit.ly, t.co, lnkd.in, a /redirect?url= address) instead of linking directly.
why: Visitors can't see where the link goes before they click, the redirect adds a delay, and if the shortener expires or is blocked the link breaks.
fix: Link straight to the destination. Social icons in the footer are a common place for these.
tech: a[href] on bit.ly, t.co, lnkd.in, buff.ly, ow.ly, tinyurl.com, goo.gl, rebrand.ly, is.gd, cutt.ly, shorturl.at, tiny.cc (or a subdomain), or a /redirect, /out or /go path with a url= style parameter holding an http(s) address; footer links count too

title: Your llms.txt sends assistants to pages that don't work
what: Links in /llms.txt return an error (4xx or 5xx) or redirect to a different site.
why: llms.txt is a short guide for AI assistants to your most useful pages. A dead or off-site link is the page they quote, or fail to.
fix: Update the links to the pages' current addresses, or remove the ones that no longer exist.
tech: links in /llms.txt answer 4xx or 5xx, or redirect off-site

title: Your llms.txt gives assistants an old phone number, address or hours
what: The phone number, street address or opening hours in /llms.txt disagree with the page's structured data.
why: Assistants quote llms.txt directly. An old number or old hours there is what someone hears when they ask if you're open tonight.
fix: Update llms.txt to match the structured data (or the other way round, whichever is wrong). Generate both from one source if you can.
tech: hours, telephone or address in /llms.txt differ from the page's LocalBusiness JSON-LD

title: Menu items go to the homepage
what: Links in the menu or header point at the homepage but are labelled as something else, such as Services or Contact.
why: Visitors who click Services land back on the homepage and think the page is missing. It usually means a menu item was added with no link.
fix: Point each menu item at its own page, or remove it until the page exists.
tech: a nav or header a[href] resolving to / whose text (or aria-label) is not Home or the site's name

title: Shared links may show no picture
what: og:image is a relative address (like /previews/landing.webp), not a full https:// address.
why: Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack and iMessage need a full address. With a relative one, shares of the page show no picture.
fix: Write og:image as a full address, including https:// and the domain. Most frameworks have a site URL setting for this.
tech: og:image does not start with http:// or https:// (protocol-relative // addresses are flagged too)

title: Shared links point at a different page than search engines see
what: The page's og:url (the address social apps use when it is shared) differs from its canonical tag.
why: Likes and shares are counted against one address while search engines rank another, and a share can open the wrong page.
fix: Set og:url to the same address as the canonical tag. Both usually come from one SEO component.
tech: og:url and <link rel="canonical"> differ by scheme, host, path or query (a trailing slash is not a difference)

title: This page is heavy to load
what: The HTML plus the images Gaugeline sampled add up to over 3 MB, and that is a floor: unsampled files come on top.
why: On a phone connection a page this heavy takes many seconds and costs visitors data.
fix: Start with the largest files in the evidence: resize and compress images, and trim the HTML's inline data.
tech: HTML bytes plus the Content-Length of sampled images (the files the run already requested) is over 3 MB (3,145,728 bytes); no extra requests are made

title: The page shows placeholder images
what: Images on the page come from a placeholder service such as placehold.co, dummyimage.com or picsum.photos.
why: Visitors see grey boxes or random stock photos where the real product or team picture should be.
fix: Upload the real images and point the img tags at them.
tech: img src on placehold.co, placehold.it, placeholder.com, via.placeholder.com, dummyimage.com, picsum.photos, placekitten.com, placebear.com, loremflickr.com, fakeimg.pl, placeimg.com, lorempixel.com (or a subdomain)

title: The page still has placeholder text
what: The page shows unfinished copy: lorem ipsum, TODO or TBD, a [bracketed placeholder], or a title or main heading such as Untitled, Staging or Test.
why: Visitors see an unfinished site, and search engines may show the placeholder in results.
fix: Replace the placeholder with the real copy. Search the CMS for "lorem", "TODO" and "[" before publishing.
tech: main content text matches "lorem ipsum", TODO/TBD/FIXME or [insert ...]-style brackets (code and pre ignored), or the whole title or h1 is one of "untitled", "untitled page", "untitled document", "new page", "page title", "title", "test", "test page", "testing", "staging", "staging site", "my site", "my website", "site title", "home page title" (English lists)

title: Your address takes several jumps to load
what: The address you entered redirects more than once before the page loads.
why: Each jump slows the first visit and can weaken how search engines credit the page.
fix: Point every redirect straight at the final address.
tech: more than one 3xx hop on the entered URL

title: A breadcrumb ends on a different page
what: The last item of a page's breadcrumb structured data points at an address other than the page's own canonical.
why: The trail should end where the visitor is. One that ends elsewhere usually means the breadcrumb was copied from another page.
fix: Make the last ListItem's item the page's canonical address, or leave the last item's URL out.
tech: the highest-position ListItem has a URL that differs from the canonical (or the page address) by scheme, host, path or query; needs a gaugeline.schema.json

title: Structured data refers to something that isn't there
what: A structured data reference ({"@id": ...}) points at a node that is not defined on the page or on the other pages checked.
why: Search engines can't follow the reference, so whatever it stands for (the publisher, the author, the organization) is lost.
fix: Define the node the reference names (usually on the homepage), or correct the @id to the one you use.
tech: an object with only an @id resolves (after normalisation) to no @id defined on the sampled pages

title: Pages redefine your organization instead of referring to it
what: Pages other than the homepage define the Organization or WebSite again, with its properties, instead of referring to the one node by its @id as your schema guide says.
why: Copies drift: one page gets an old logo or phone number, and search engines see several organizations where there should be one.
fix: On every other page, write {"@id": "<the configured id>"} where the Organization or WebSite is needed, and define it once on the homepage.
tech: an Organization or WebSite node with properties beyond @id and @type on a page other than / (needs organizationId or websiteId in gaugeline.schema.json)

title: A page is missing structured data its template requires
what: A page that matches one of your schema guide's templates (for example /blog/*) lacks a type the guide requires there, such as Article or BreadcrumbList.
why: Rich results for that kind of page depend on the type, and one template that drifted usually means every page built from it did.
fix: Add the missing type to the template's structured data component.
tech: the most specific matching template's require list has a type missing from the page's JSON-LD (@type anywhere, @graph included); common subtypes count (an AboutPage is a WebPage, a BlogPosting an Article); needs templates in gaugeline.schema.json

title: Your sitemap lists pages on a different address
what: Every entry in the sitemap uses a different host than the site, for example a staging domain or the other of www and the bare domain.
why: Search engines ignore sitemap entries for a host the sitemap does not belong to, so the sitemap does nothing for this site.
fix: Generate the sitemap with the site's public address. In most frameworks this is a site URL or base URL setting.
tech: every sitemap entry's host differs from the page's host

title: Search engines can't find a list of your pages
what: There is no sitemap at /sitemap.xml, and robots.txt does not say where one is.
why: Without a sitemap, search engines find pages only by following links, so new or deep pages take longer to appear.
fix: Publish a sitemap at /sitemap.xml (most site builders and frameworks can generate one) and add a Sitemap: line with its full address to robots.txt.
tech: /sitemap.xml is not a 200 sitemap and robots.txt has no Sitemap: line

title: Your sitemap lists old addresses that redirect
what: Pages listed in the sitemap answer with a redirect (3xx) instead of the page.
why: A sitemap should list the final address of each page. Redirecting entries make search engines do extra work and can keep the old address in results.
fix: List each page at the address it redirects to. This often follows a move to https, to www, or to a new URL scheme.
tech: sampled sitemap entries return 3xx

title: The same structured data is on this page twice
what: A schema.org type is described both in JSON-LD and as microdata (itemtype) on the same page.
why: Search engines see two descriptions of one thing, which can disagree, and may pick the wrong one or ignore both.
fix: Keep one: usually the JSON-LD, and remove the itemscope and itemtype attributes from the theme or plugin that adds microdata.
tech: a schema.org @type in JSON-LD is also a microdata itemtype

title: This page isn't set up for phone screens
what: The page has no viewport meta tag, so phones show it zoomed out as if on a desktop screen.
why: Visitors have to pinch and zoom to read anything, and Google treats the page as not mobile-friendly.
fix: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the page's head.
tech: no <meta name="viewport"> anywhere in the document

title: Some AI assistants can't read your site
what: robots.txt stops one or more known AI crawlers from reading the home page. Gaugeline says which, and whether the block names them or comes from a rule for every crawler.
why: People ask assistants about a business before they open its site. Blocking AI crawlers is a fair choice; blocking them by accident means assistants answer from old or second-hand information.
fix: If the block is on purpose, there is nothing to do. If it comes from a Disallow: / meant for a staging site, remove it, or add groups for the assistants you want to allow.
tech: known AI user-agent tokens (packages/core/src/data/ai-agents.json) are disallowed / by robots.txt

title: The store lists the app under a different name
what: The name the App Store or Google Play shows for a linked app differs from the name you expect.
why: A renamed or replaced app can mean the link points at an old listing, or at someone else's app.
fix: Check the link points at the right listing. If the app was renamed on purpose, update the expected name.
tech: the store's app name differs from the expected app name (case, punctuation and a leading "The" ignored); only runs when an expected name is set

title: The page doesn't say which address is the real one
what: There's no canonical tag.
why: Copies of the page with tracking parameters can be treated as separate pages.
fix: Add a self-referencing canonical tag.
tech: no <link rel="canonical">

title: Some events are missing details search engines need
what: An event in the page's structured data has no start date, no location or no event status.
why: Google needs these to show the event in results, and the status is how a cancelled or moved night is shown as such.
fix: Give every Event a startDate, a location and an eventStatus (for example https://schema.org/EventScheduled).
tech: Event JSON-LD without startDate, location or eventStatus (one finding listing each event and what it lacks)

title: Some language codes are not valid
what: hreflang uses a code that isn't a valid language tag (such as "sp" or "es_US"), or a page with three or more languages has no x-default.
why: Search engines ignore an hreflang with an invalid code, and without x-default they guess which version to show everyone else.
fix: Use BCP 47 codes such as es, es-US or es-419 (a hyphen, not an underscore), and add hreflang="x-default" for the version to show when no language matches.
tech: an hreflang value is not a BCP 47 tag (two-letter languages must be ISO 639-1), or 3+ distinct languages have no x-default

title: Some images have no alt attribute
what: Some images have no alt attribute at all, not even an empty one.
why: Without alt, screen readers read the file name aloud. An empty alt="" tells them to skip a decorative image; a missing one does not.
fix: Add alt to every img: a short description, or alt="" for decorative images.
tech: img elements with no alt attribute (one finding with a count and the first three)

title: Images use older, heavier file formats
what: Images are served as JPEG, PNG or GIF with no WebP or AVIF version offered.
why: WebP and AVIF are usually a quarter to a half smaller for the same picture, so the page loads faster.
fix: Offer WebP or AVIF with a <picture> element or srcset, or let your image CDN or framework image component pick the format.
tech: a sampled image's Content-Type is image/jpeg, image/png or image/gif and it has no WebP or AVIF candidate (SVG is never reported)

title: A language version declares the wrong language
what: A version's <html lang> names a different language than the version is (for example the Spanish page still says lang="en").
why: Screen readers read the page with the wrong voice and pronunciation, and browsers offer to translate it into its own language.
fix: Set <html lang> per version from the page's language, usually in the layout component.
tech: <html lang>'s primary subtag differs from the version's language (from hreflang or the configured scheme)

title: Some text wasn't translated
what: Strings you listed as default-language text (button labels, headings) appear on another language version.
why: A Spanish page with an English "Add to cart" button looks unfinished, and some visitors won't know what it does.
fix: Translate the strings in the components that render them; they are usually hard-coded in a shared button or heading.
tech: a string from untranslated in gaugeline.languages.json appears in another version's main text or link names (case ignored); needs the list

title: Some links don't say where they go
what: Links whose whole text is "read more", "click here", "learn more" or "here".
why: Screen reader users often browse a page by its links, and hear a list of identical "read more"s. Search engines also read link text to understand the destination.
fix: Make the link text name the destination, such as "Read more about pricing", or add an aria-label that does.
tech: a link's accessible name (aria-label, else its text) is exactly "read more", "click here", "learn more", "here" (English list)

title: Links on this page go through a redirect
what: Links to other pages on the site answer with a redirect (3xx) before reaching the page.
why: Each redirect adds a round trip for visitors, and search engines pass a little less on through every hop.
fix: Change the link to the address it ends up at. This usually follows a move to new URLs, https or www.
tech: a sampled same-site a[href] answers 3xx first and ends in 200

title: One page has two names in your menus
what: The same link appears in the menu, header or footer with two different labels.
why: Visitors wonder whether the two labels are two pages, and the site reads as unfinished.
fix: Use one label for each page everywhere. Menus kept in two places (a header and a footer component) drift apart first.
tech: one href (a #fragment makes a different destination) has more than one distinct label across nav, header and footer (case and trailing arrows ignored)

title: Shared links have no picture
what: The page has no og:image tag.
why: When the page is shared in a chat or a social post, it shows as a plain link with no picture, which fewer people click.
fix: Add <meta property="og:image" content="https://..."> with a 1200 by 630 picture for the page.
tech: no og:image (or og:image:url) meta property

title: Breadcrumbs don't start where your guide says
what: The first item of a page's breadcrumb structured data is not the Home name and address your schema guide sets.
why: Search results show the breadcrumb trail; one that starts somewhere else on some pages looks inconsistent and can point at the wrong page.
fix: Start every BreadcrumbList with the configured first item, for example Home at /.
tech: the lowest-position ListItem's name or URL differs from breadcrumbs.firstName / breadcrumbs.firstUrl in gaugeline.schema.json (name case ignored, URL resolved)

title: A phone link may not dial correctly
what: A tel: link has spaces or brackets in the number.
why: Some phones and click-to-call tools dial the wrong number, or nothing, when the link has spaces or brackets.
fix: Write the link as digits with a leading + and country code, for example href="tel:+14155550100". Keep the spaced format in the visible text only.
tech: an a[href^="tel:"] contains a space, ( or ); "-" and "." pass. One finding per distinct number
